cloze.text: Breaking {{c1::any one}} link of the chain of infection stops the transmission.
An infectious agent can be {{c1::bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, or parasites::5 kinds}}.
Some agents are highly infectious and spread easily between hosts (e.g., {{c1::measles}}, COVID-19); others cause disease only in {{c2::immunocompromised}} individuals.
Common infectious agents in dentistry: {{c1::hepatitis B virus}}, herpes simplex virus, {{c2::Mycobacterium tuberculosis}}, and HIV.
{{c1::Vehicles}} are substances that can carry and transmit an infectious agent, such as food, water, blood, or fomites.
A vehicle may simply carry a pathogen (e.g., {{c1::hepatitis A}} in contaminated food) or support its growth and toxin production (e.g., {{c2::Clostridium botulinum}} in improperly canned food).
{{c1::Vectors}} are living organisms, such as mosquitoes, fleas, or ticks, that can transmit pathogens.
The reservoir is not always the source of infection: C. botulinum lives in {{c1::soil}}, but infections come from {{c2::improperly canned food}}.
Humans are the reservoir for many common diseases seen in dentistry, including {{c1::strep throat}}, influenza, tuberculosis, and COVID-19.
{{c1::Carriers}} can transmit disease without showing symptoms.
Smallpox could be eradicated because {{c1::humans were its only reservoir}}.
cloze.extra: Once infections were eliminated from people, the virus had nowhere left to survive.

cloze.text: {{c1::Zoonoses}} are diseases that spread from animals to humans (e.g., rabies, HIV, COVID-19 — likely from bats).
Water can be an environmental reservoir: {{c1::Legionella pneumophila}} is found in {{c2::dental unit waterlines}} that are not properly maintained.
The portal of exit is often the same as the portal of {{c1::entry}} — e.g., influenza, COVID-19, and TB exit and enter through the {{c2::respiratory tract}}.
Pathogens can exit through saliva, blood, respiratory droplets, feces, urine, or other body fluids; in dentistry the common exits are {{c1::saliva}}, {{c1::respiratory droplets}}, and {{c1::blood}}.
Some agents exit through cuts, wounds, or {{c1::contaminated sharps}} (e.g., {{c2::hepatitis B}}).
Some agents exit through the {{c1::placenta}} from mother to fetus (e.g., rubella, syphilis, toxoplasmosis).
SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) is primarily spread through {{c1::droplets}} released when a person coughs, sneezes, or talks.
{{c1::Direct contact}} transmission is the physical transfer of a pathogen, e.g., touching blood, saliva, or open lesions.
{{c1::Indirect contact}} transmission occurs via a contaminated object or surface (fomite), e.g., instruments, gloves, handpieces, countertops, door handles, charts, bedding.
In {{c1::droplet}} transmission, large respiratory droplets (e.g., from coughing or sneezing) travel {{c2::short}} distances and land on mucous membranes (eyes, nose, mouth).
In {{c1::airborne}} transmission, smaller particles remain suspended in the air and are inhaled (e.g., tuberculosis, measles).
{{c1::Common vehicle}} transmission is spread through contaminated food, water, or medication shared by many people.
{{c1::Vector-borne}} transmission is spread through insects or animals (e.g., mosquitoes transmitting malaria) — not common in dentistry.
In dental settings, the most common modes of transmission are {{c1::direct contact}}, {{c1::indirect contact}}, and {{c1::droplet}} transmission.
Pathogens can enter through the {{c1::mouth, nose, eyes, skin, or mucous membranes::5 sites}}.
The {{c1::respiratory tract}} is a common portal of entry in dentistry due to aerosols and droplets.
The {{c1::fecal-oral route}} involves pathogens exiting in feces and entering through the mouth via contaminated food or water (e.g., {{c2::polio}}).
cloze.extra: Fecal-oral transmission: microorganisms spread from human or animal stool to the mouth.

cloze.text: Bloodborne agents (e.g., hepatitis B) can enter through cuts, needle sticks, open wounds, {{c1::transfusions}}, sharps injuries, or mucosal contact.
A host's susceptibility depends on their immune system, health status, {{c1::genetics}}, {{c2::age}}, and vaccination history.
More susceptible due to weaker immune defenses: immunocompromised individuals (cancer, HIV, chemotherapy), {{c1::unvaccinated}} individuals, the {{c2::elderly}}, and the very young.
Some genetic traits protect: people with the {{c1::sickle cell trait}} are partially protected from {{c2::malaria}}.
Good health habits, {{c1::hand hygiene}}, {{c2::PPE}}, and {{c3::vaccination}} reduce a host's susceptibility.
In direct contact transmission, microorganisms pass from one infected person to another without a {{c1::contaminated object or person}} in between.
Direct contact occurs through skin-to-skin contact, kissing, sexual activity, or contact with {{c1::mucous membranes or non-intact skin}} (e.g., cuts or abrasions).
Diseases spread by direct contact include herpes simplex virus, HIV, hepatitis B, and {{c1::infectious mononucleosis}} ("kissing disease").
In dentistry, exposure to a patient's blood or saliva through a cut on the clinician's hand is {{c1::direct}} transmission.
In dental settings, {{c1::hepatitis B and C}} can spread when blood or saliva from one patient contaminates a surface or tool that is then touched by another person.
Proper {{c1::sterilization}} of instruments, {{c2::disinfection}} of surfaces, and hand hygiene are critical in preventing indirect contact transmission.
Particle size: droplet transmission {{c1::> 10 microns}}; airborne transmission {{c2::< 10 microns}}.

Airborne transmission is caused by {{c1::droplet nuclei}} — tiny particles smaller than 10 microns (often < 5 microns) that form when larger respiratory droplets {{c2::evaporate}}, leaving behind infectious material.
In the air, droplets {{c1::fall quickly to the ground}}, whereas airborne particles {{c2::remain suspended for hours}}.
Airborne transmission is {{c1::long}} range — it can travel across a room or through ventilation.
Droplets spread by coughing, sneezing, and talking and may contact mucosa; airborne particles are {{c1::inhaled deep into the lungs}} from aerosols or droplet nuclei.
Droplets can settle on surfaces and transfer by touch; airborne particles are less likely to settle, so the main concern is {{c1::inhalation}}.
COVID-19 spreads by {{c1::droplet}} transmission in typical cases but by {{c2::airborne}} transmission during aerosol-generating procedures.
Influenza, {{c1::mumps}}, {{c1::rubella}}, and herpesviruses are spread by droplet transmission.
Tuberculosis, {{c1::measles}}, and {{c2::chickenpox}} are spread by airborne transmission.
Protection needed: droplet transmission → {{c1::surgical mask}} and standard precautions; airborne transmission → {{c2::N95 respirator}} or higher and airborne precautions.
N95 masks filter ≥ {{c1::95%}} of particles down to {{c2::0.3 microns}}.
Particle sizes: viruses = {{c1::0.02–0.3}} µm; bacteria = {{c2::0.5–10}} µm; spores = {{c3::0.5–30}} µm.

Dental relevance: droplets come from speaking, coughing, or {{c1::spatter}} from procedures; airborne aerosols are generated by {{c2::ultrasonic scaling}}, high-speed handpieces, and {{c3::air polishing}}.
{{c1::Bloodborne}} transmission: microorganisms spread through blood and other body fluids.
Three of the most common bloodborne pathogens health care workers are at risk from: HIV, {{c1::hepatitis B virus (HBV)}}, and {{c2::hepatitis C virus (HCV)}}.

Health care workers are exposed to bloodborne diseases in two ways: a {{c1::percutaneous}} injury (injured by a sharp object) or a {{c2::mucocutaneous}} exposure (mucous membrane or non-intact skin contacts blood, tissue, or other potentially infectious body fluids).
In {{c1::food and water}} transmission, microorganisms spread through contaminated food; improper food storage, contaminated water, or fecal material can be responsible.
{{c1::Standard precautions}} are infection control practices used with {{c2::all patients}}, regardless of their known or suspected infection status.
Standard precautions assume blood, saliva, all body fluids (except {{c1::sweat}}), non-intact skin, and mucous membranes may be infectious, even in {{c2::asymptomatic}} patients.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "Be A Smart Nurse, Man!" = Blood, All body fluids (except sweat), Saliva, Non-intact skin, Mucous membranes.

cloze.text: Under standard precautions, "blood" means visible or {{c1::microscopic}}, and body fluids, secretions, and excretions count {{c2::whether or not they contain blood}}.
cloze.extra: Saliva is especially relevant in dental settings; non-intact skin = rashes, cuts, abrasions; mucous membranes = eyes, nose, mouth.

cloze.text: Standard precautions in dentistry include using {{c1::rubber dams}} and {{c2::high-volume evacuation}} to reduce aerosol spread.
cloze.extra: Also: gloves, mask, protective eyewear and gown for all procedures; sterilizing instruments between patients; hand hygiene before and after patient contact; disinfecting operatory surfaces after each use.

cloze.text: Treat all patients' saliva and blood as if they contain {{c1::HIV, HBV, or HCV}}, even without a confirmed diagnosis.
{{c1::Universal precautions}} were introduced in the {{c2::1980s}} to protect healthcare workers from bloodborne pathogens, especially HIV and hepatitis B.
Universal precautions focused only on {{c1::blood and specific high-risk body fluids}} (e.g., semen, vaginal secretions); {{c2::saliva}} and other non-bloody fluids were not included.
cloze.extra: Don't be confused! Universal precautions = blood only. Standard precautions = blood + saliva + all body fluids + non-intact skin + mucous membranes.

cloze.text: In the {{c1::1990s}}, the CDC replaced universal precautions with standard precautions to provide broader protection.
Standard precautions are the current {{c1::CDC}} guideline used in all healthcare settings, including hospitals and dental offices.
HIV is transmitted through blood, semen, vaginal and rectal fluids, and {{c1::breast milk}} — only on contact with {{c2::mucous membranes, non-intact skin, or by injection}}.
HIV is not spread through {{c1::saliva}}, aerosols, or casual contact.
In dentistry, HIV exposure risk comes from {{c1::needlestick injuries}} or contact with infected blood through cuts or mucosa.
{{c1::Standard precautions}} are sufficient to prevent HIV transmission in dental settings.
PPE protects the clinician's {{c1::skin}} and the mucous membranes of the {{c2::eyes, nose, and mouth}} from blood, saliva, and other potentially infectious materials.
PPE includes gloves, masks, {{c1::safety glasses or face shields}}, and gowns.
Protective clothing should prevent contamination of street clothes, have fitted {{c1::cuffs and necklines}}, and be removed by {{c2::rolling it inside out}}.
Gloves must be changed between patients or if {{c1::torn}}, must never be worn {{c2::outside the operatory}}, and should cover the gown cuffs.
Surgical masks should filter at least {{c1::95%}} of bacteria, be sealed around the nose, sides, and chin, and be changed between every patient or when {{c2::moist}}.
Remove a mask by handling it by its {{c1::strings or elastic}} (straps).
Surgical masks do not protect against {{c1::airborne}} transmission (e.g., tuberculosis) — an N95 respirator or higher is needed.
{{c1::Hand hygiene}} is the general term that applies to handwashing, antiseptic hand rubs, or surgical hand antiseptics.
Wearing gloves {{c1::is not a substitute}} for routine handwashing.
Hands must be washed before and after the use of gloves, and {{c1::between patients}}.
For handwashing, vigorously lather plain soap and dry with {{c1::towels}}; nails must be kept {{c2::short and clean}}.
Watches, bracelets, and rings must be removed to prevent {{c1::harboring microorganisms}}.
Alcohol-based hand rubs can be used when {{c1::no visible soil}} is on the hands.

{{c1::Transient}} flora lives on the skin surface, is picked up from patients and surfaces, and is easily removed with handwashing; {{c2::resident}} flora is attached to deeper skin layers, more resistant to removal, and less likely to cause infections.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: transient = someone just passing through (short stay, easily washed off); resident = someone with a long-term lease or mortgage.

cloze.text: Needle-stick injuries are a {{c1::major}} cause of disease transmission to health care personnel.
Recap needles with the {{c1::scoop}} technique, not the {{c2::two-handed}} technique.
Recap needles between use and before disposal, and {{c1::never bend or break}} needles before disposal.

Immunizations protect both the patient and the health care professional; required vaccinations include hepatitis B, influenza, varicella, measles, mumps, polio, rubella (German measles), and {{c1::tetanus}}.
Hepatitis B vaccine schedule: second injection {{c1::1 month}} after the first; third injection {{c2::6 months}} after the first.
The Mantoux tuberculin skin test should be administered {{c1::annually}}.
No vaccine exists for {{c1::HIV}} or {{c1::hepatitis C}}.
Obtain, review, and update clients' health histories at {{c1::every}} visit.
The clinician can {{c1::refuse}} to treat a patient with a susceptible communicable illness — e.g., patients with {{c2::active TB}} should be declined and referred to a physician.
{{c1::Pre-procedural antimicrobial mouth rinses}} temporarily reduce the number of microorganisms in the oral cavity, especially before aerosol-generating procedures.
According to the ADA and CDC, pre-procedural rinses can reduce the microbial load in saliva by up to {{c1::94%}}, though evidence that this reduces infection risk is {{c2::inconclusive}}.
Common pre-procedural rinse agents: {{c1::0.12%}} chlorhexidine, {{c2::1%}} hydrogen peroxide, and {{c3::0.2%}} povidone-iodine.
cloze.extra: Choice depends on clinical preference and patient tolerance.

cloze.text: {{c1::Biohazard waste}} (e.g., blood-soaked gauze, soft tissue) goes in a leak-resistant biohazard bag with a biohazard label; gauze with minimal blood is {{c2::household waste}}.
Sharps must be disposed of in {{c1::puncture-resistant}} containers marked with a biohazard label.
Most routine dental waste — patient bibs, barriers, PPE, items not saturated with blood or saliva — can be discarded as {{c1::regular trash}}.
Disposing of small amounts of blood and fluids into {{c1::sanitary sewers}} is considered safe; there is no evidence of disease transmission through sewage.
cloze.extra: Follow local regulations on whether blood or fluids must be pre-treated.

cloze.text: Extracted teeth are considered potentially infectious by {{c1::OSHA}} and go in medical waste containers, but may be {{c2::returned to the patient}} upon request.
Amalgam must never go in biohazard bags, trash, or incinerated waste, or be flushed down drains; it must be {{c1::collected and recycled}} separately per local environmental regulations.
Dental unit waterlines can become colonized by bacteria, fungi, and {{c1::protozoa}} if not properly maintained.
Flush waterlines for {{c1::2 minutes}} at the start of the day and for {{c2::20–30 seconds}} between patients.
During a boil-water advisory, avoid using public water in dental equipment and use {{c1::bottled or distilled}} water.
{{c1::Cleaning}} is the essential first step of any disinfection or sterilization; it removes blood, debris, and organic matter that interfere with the process.
Sterile means {{c1::free from all living microorganisms}}; a {{c2::sterilant}} produces this effect.

A {{c1::disinfectant}} is a germicide used on {{c2::inanimate objects}} (floors, walls, sinks) to destroy all recognized pathogenic microorganisms, but not necessarily all bacterial {{c3::endospores}}.
High-level disinfectants are regulated by the {{c1::FDA}}; intermediate- and low-level disinfectants are registered with the {{c2::EPA}}.
Intermediate-level disinfectants are EPA-registered {{c1::with}} a tuberculocidal claim; low-level disinfectants are EPA-registered {{c2::without}} a tuberculocidal claim.
High-level disinfectants kill bacteria, M. tuberculosis, fungi, and viruses but not {{c1::high numbers of bacterial spores}}.
Intermediate-level disinfectants kill bacteria, M. tuberculosis, most fungi, and viruses but not {{c1::bacterial spores}}.
Low-level disinfectants kill most bacteria, some fungi, and viruses but not {{c1::M. tuberculosis}} and spores.
Used on: high-level → {{c1::medical devices}} (not environmental surfaces); intermediate-level → {{c2::environmental (clinical contact) surfaces}}; low-level → {{c3::housekeeping surfaces}}.
High-level disinfectant example: {{c1::glutaraldehyde}} ({{c2::10}}-hour immersion).
Intermediate-level examples: {{c1::iodophors}}, {{c1::phenolics}}, {{c1::chlorine compounds}}, and some quats; low-level examples: {{c2::alcohol-free quats}} and household disinfectants.
{{c1::Critical}} items penetrate soft tissue or bone, or contact the bloodstream (e.g., curettes, needles, surgical burs), and require {{c2::heat sterilization}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Critical → C like Curette, C like Cut (through the mucous membrane). Semi-critical → S like Stroke (to touch). Non-critical → non-contact with the mucous membrane.

cloze.text: {{c1::Semi-critical}} items contact mucous membranes or non-intact skin but do not penetrate (e.g., radiographic receptor holders, mouth mirrors, reusable impression trays), and require {{c2::heat sterilization or high-level disinfection}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Critical → C like Curette, C like Cut (through the mucous membrane). Semi-critical → S like Stroke (to touch). Non-critical → non-contact with the mucous membrane. (The book says "film holders"; the exam uses "image receptor".)

cloze.text: {{c1::Non-critical}} items contact intact skin only (e.g., blood pressure cuff, x-ray tube head) and require {{c2::intermediate- or low-level disinfection}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Critical → C like Curette, C like Cut (through the mucous membrane). Semi-critical → S like Stroke (to touch). Non-critical → non-contact with the mucous membrane.

cloze.text: {{c1::Clinical}} surfaces (light handles, switches, pens, countertops) do not touch the patient directly but pose a moderate risk and must be disinfected between patients with an {{c2::intermediate- or low-level}} disinfectant.
{{c1::Housekeeping}} surfaces (floors, sinks) have minimal risk and can be cleaned with {{c2::detergent and water}} only.
A {{c1::surfactant}} is a cleaning agent that loosens, emulsifies, and suspends organisms so they can be rinsed away.
{{c1::Ultrasonic cleaning}} is the preferred method of cleaning instruments; it uses {{c2::cavitation}}, in which vibrating bubbles dislodge contaminants from instrument surfaces.

basic.back: Inanimate objects that can carry a pathogen (e.g., instruments, gloves, bedding)
The habitat in which the agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies — can be human, animal, or the environment
basic.extra: e.g., soil is the reservoir of Clostridium botulinum

basic.back: The path by which a pathogen leaves its host (its previous home)
basic.extra: e.g., influenza viruses and Mycobacterium tuberculosis exit through the respiratory tract

basic.back: The way a pathogen moves from one host (or the environment) to another
The "entrance" the pathogen uses to get inside the new host (its new home)
The average number of people one infected person can transmit the disease to

basic.front: Why is measles the most contagious human virus known?
basic.back: It spreads through airborne droplet nuclei that stay in the air for hours.

basic.front: Why was the shift from universal to standard precautions especially important for dental professionals?
basic.back: Because of their constant exposure to saliva, aerosols, and blood — saliva was not covered by universal precautions.

basic.front: Why shouldn't petroleum-based lotions be used with latex gloves?
basic.back: Latex is natural rubber and petroleum acts as a solvent — it weakens the glove so it tears or leaks more easily (often unnoticed).

basic.front: Why shouldn't a patient seal their lips completely around the saliva ejector?
basic.back: It can create backflow, increasing the risk of cross-contamination.

basic.front: Why must an amalgam-filled extracted tooth not go in the trash or a biohazard bag?
basic.back: It can release mercury, a neurotoxin that harms the brain, kidneys, and environment; incinerated or landfilled, mercury can enter the air, soil, or water supply.
Destruction of ALL microorganisms, including spores, by physical or chemical means
Destruction of pathogenic and other microorganisms by physical or chemical means — less lethal than sterilization
A substance applied to living tissue/skin that stops or slows the growth of microorganisms (e.g., alcohols, chlorhexidine, triclosan)
Absence of bacteria, viruses, and other microorganisms

typein.question: How many essential links make up the chain of infection?
typein.extra: Agent → reservoir → portal of exit → mode of transmission → portal of entry → susceptible host

typein.question: In what year did the World Health Organization declare smallpox eradicated?
typein.extra: After a global vaccination campaign; the last known natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977.

typein.question: Droplet transmission is short range — typically up to how many feet?
typein.extra: ≤ 3 feet / 1 meter. Airborne transmission is long range (across a room or via ventilation).

typein.question: Risk of HIV transmission after a needlestick with HIV-positive blood (percent)?
typein.extra: Very low. Standard precautions are sufficient to prevent HIV transmission in dental settings.

typein.question: Alcohol hand rubs in what concentration range (%) are more effective at killing germs?
typein.extra: More effective than lower-concentration or non-alcohol hand sanitizers.

typein.question: How many injections does the hepatitis B vaccination series require?
Hepatitis B virus can survive in dried blood on surfaces — and remain infectious — for at least how many days?

mcq.question: A dental unit waterline that has not been properly maintained becomes colonized with Legionella pneumophila. In the chain of infection, the waterline is the:
mcq.explanation: A reservoir is the habitat where the agent lives, grows and multiplies — here an environmental (water) reservoir. Legionella itself is the agent; a vector is a living organism such as a mosquito.

mcq.question: A hygienist handles a patient chart with contaminated gloves; later the receptionist touches the chart and then rubs her eyes. Which mode of transmission does this illustrate?
mcq.explanation: The pathogen passed via a contaminated object (fomite) — the chart — so it is indirect contact. Direct contact would need person-to-person transfer with no object in between.

mcq.question: A dental office requires all staff to be vaccinated against hepatitis B. Which link of the chain of infection does this mainly break?
mcq.explanation: Vaccination lowers the susceptibility of the potential new host. Mode of transmission is broken by measures such as sterilization, disinfection and hand hygiene.

mcq.question: Which dental procedure is most likely to generate airborne (aerosol) transmission of pathogens?
options: C. Hand scaling with a curette
mcq.explanation: Ultrasonic scaling, high-speed handpieces and air polishing generate aerosols (droplet nuclei < 10 µm) that stay suspended. Hand scaling produces spatter (droplets), not significant aerosol.

mcq.question: During scaling, a patient's blood splashes into the hygienist's unprotected eye. This exposure is classified as:
mcq.explanation: Contact of blood with a mucous membrane (the eye) or non-intact skin is a mucocutaneous exposure. A percutaneous injury requires a sharp object piercing the skin.

mcq.question: Under standard precautions, each of the following is treated as potentially infectious EXCEPT:
mcq.explanation: Standard precautions cover blood, all body fluids except sweat, saliva, non-intact skin and mucous membranes ("Be A Smart Nurse, Man"). Saliva was the big addition over universal precautions.

mcq.question: A hygienist applies a petroleum-based hand cream between patients and then dons latex gloves. What is the most likely consequence?
options: A. The gloves fit more tightly and improve tactile sense
B. The petroleum weakens the latex, so the gloves tear or leak more easily
C. The cream disinfects the hands under the gloves
D. There is no effect on latex
mcq.answer: B. The petroleum weakens the latex, so the gloves tear or leak more easily
mcq.explanation: Petroleum acts as a solvent on natural-rubber latex, weakening it. Use water- or silicone-based lotions instead.

mcq.question: Which instruction about the saliva ejector best reduces the risk of cross-contamination?
options: A. Ask the patient to close their lips tightly around the tip
B. Do not let the patient seal their lips around the tip
C. Turn off the saliva ejector while the patient closes
D. Use a pre-procedural rinse instead of the saliva ejector
mcq.answer: B. Do not let the patient seal their lips around the tip
mcq.explanation: Sealing the lips around the saliva ejector can create backflow of fluid from the suction line into the mouth, increasing cross-contamination.

mcq.question: A disinfectant's label states it is EPA-registered with a tuberculocidal claim. Which level of disinfectant is it?
mcq.explanation: Intermediate-level = EPA-registered WITH a tuberculocidal claim (kills M. tuberculosis but not spores). High-level disinfectants are FDA-regulated; low-level have no tuberculocidal claim.

mcq.question: A reusable item contacts only the patient's intact skin. What is the minimum processing it requires?
mcq.explanation: Items touching intact skin only are non-critical (e.g., BP cuff) → intermediate- or low-level disinfection. Heat sterilization or high-level disinfection is for semi-critical items.
